turns.text: What's the best way to start a campfire if the wood is a bit damp?

turns.text: Split the logs to get at the dry wood inside, and start with lots of small dry kindling. Birch bark or a few cotton balls with petroleum jelly catch really well.

turns.text: It does. They burn for a few minutes, which gives the damp twigs time to dry and catch.

turns.text: Okay, and how big should the fire be / if we just want to make some tea?

turns.text: Small is better for cooking. A compact bed of hot coals heats a pot much more evenly than big flames.

turns.text: Good to know. How do I put it out properly before bed?

turns.text: Drown it with water, stir the ashes, and drown it again. If it's still warm to the back of your hand, keep going.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's it. Door facing away from the wind too, if you can.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How do I keep stuff in a cooler cold for a whole long weekend?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Start with a cold cooler. Bring it inside the night before, and if you can, chill it with a bag of ice first.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Huh, never thought of that. Ice cubes or blocks?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Blocks last much longer. Frozen water bottles work great too, and you can drink them when they melt.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Smart. Anything else?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Keep drinks in a separate cooler. People open the drinks one constantly, and every opening lets the cold out.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Oh, that's exactly what kills ours. My brother opens it every ten minutes.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then give him his own cooler. Also keep it in the shade and throw a blanket over it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Should I drain the melted water?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Leave it in while it's icy, it actually helps. Drain it once it starts getting warm.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Is it crazy to take a ten month old camping?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Not crazy at all. Lots of families do it. It just takes a bit more planning, especially around sleep.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Sleep is my big fear. He barely sleeps at home.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Bring whatever is part of his routine, the same sleeping bag or blanket, a familiar song. Familiar smells help a lot in a new place.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And what about the cold at night? / I keep picturing him freezing.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Dress him in layers rather than piling blankets on him. A baby sleeping bag over warm pajamas is ideal, and feel the back of his neck to check.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay. Any tips for daytime?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A travel playpen gives him a safe spot while you cook. And go somewhere close to home first, so you can bail if it's a disaster.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That makes me feel much better, honestly.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What am I supposed to do with dish water at a campsite?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Strain out the food bits first and pack them out with your trash. Then scatter the water widely, at least a couple hundred feet from any stream or lake.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Even if I used eco soap?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Yes, even then. Biodegradable soap still needs soil to break down, it's not safe straight into water.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay. And the little food scraps, can I just bury them?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Better not. Animals dig them up and get used to people food. Pack them out with everything else.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That's a lot of rules for washing a pot.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Ha, it is. A trick is to scrape the pot really well and use hot water, then you barely need soap at all.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Fine, I'll be a good camper.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: The wildlife thanks you.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Give me a campfire story for kids. Spooky but not nightmare spooky.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: How about the lantern in the woods? A girl sees a light bobbing between the trees every night, and nobody believes her.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Ooh, okay, keep going.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: One night she follows it and finds an old man looking for his lost dog. He's been searching for years.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Is he a ghost?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's the twist. She helps him look, and at sunrise they find the dog, and both of them just fade away, happy. The light never comes back.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Aw. That's spooky and sweet. My youngest will cry.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then end it with the girl getting a puppy of her own. Happy tears only.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Perfect. Do you have a funny one too, / for when they're too wired to sleep?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Try the bear who borrowed a tent. He keeps zipping himself in upside down. Kids love doing the voices.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: We're camping somewhere really dark next week. How do I make the most of the stars?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Lucky you. First, check the moon. A new moon week is perfect, a full moon washes out a lot of stars.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How do I check that?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Any weather app or a quick search for the moon phase. Then give your eyes about twenty minutes in full darkness to adjust.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Twenty minutes? Seriously?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Seriously. And no phone screens, they reset your night vision. If you need light, use a red headlamp.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I have no idea what I'd even be looking at though.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A star map app can help, just switch it to night mode. Look for the Milky Way, it looks like a pale cloud across the sky.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And should I bring anything?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Reclining camp chairs or a blanket to lie on, and warm layers. Stargazing gets cold fast.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My sister keeps calling glamping real camping. It's not, right?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Ha, it's a spicy topic. Glamping is camping with comforts, proper beds, sometimes electricity. Whether it counts depends who you ask.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: She stayed in a yurt with a hot tub and a wine fridge.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Okay, that's very far on the glamour end. Still outside though, technically.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Technically. I slept on a rock in the rain last month, so / I feel like I've earned the right to judge.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: You've definitely earned bragging rights. But maybe she'll get hooked and try the rock version next time.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Doubt it. Would you count it?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: I'd say if you hear the wind and owls at night, it's camping in spirit. The hot tub is just a very nice bonus.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That's annoyingly diplomatic.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It's a gift. Tell her she owes you one rainy weekend though.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I left the tent stakes at home. We're already here and it's getting dark.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Don't panic, you can improvise. Are you on soft ground or a hard, rocky site?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Soft-ish. Lots of sticks around.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Good. Find straight, sturdy sticks about as thick as your thumb, sharpen one end with a knife or a rock, and push them in at an angle away from the tent.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Will that hold if it gets windy?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Mostly. You can also tie the guy lines to rocks, bushes or a picnic table. Heavy gear inside the corners helps too.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay, I'm finding sticks now. My partner is not impressed.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Tell them you're doing a bushcraft skills session on purpose.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Ha. She won't buy it.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Probably not. But the tent will stay up, and that's what counts tonight.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: There's thunder in the distance and we're camping on a hill. What do we do?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Take it seriously. The safest place is a hard-topped car with the windows up, not the tent. Is your car nearby?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: About five minutes' walk down.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then head there now, before it gets close. If you can hear thunder, you're within range of lightning.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Should we pack up the tent first?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: No, just grab essentials and go. The tent can get wet, it'll be fine.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay, we're walking. What if we couldn't get to the car?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Get off the high ground, away from lone trees and metal poles, and crouch low on your pad with your feet together. But the car is much better.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Made it. Rain's starting.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Good. Wait about half an hour after the last thunder before heading back up.

option_sets.lead_in: I need help picking a campsite for next month.
options: The first one is right on the beach, with showers and a little shop, but it's pretty crowded.
Then there's a site deep in the national forest, no water, no toilets, totally quiet.
And the last one is a family campground by a river, with a playground and fire pits at every spot.
moshi_comment: If you want comfort, the beach site wins with its showers, but the crowds might bother you. The forest site is the most peaceful, though you'd have to carry all your water. Who's coming along?
The river campground sounds like a nice middle ground, fire pits and some facilities without the beach crowds. I'd only pick the forest site if you're happy to rough it completely.

option_sets.lead_in: We can't agree on how to sleep on our camping trip, so help me decide.
options: Option one is our old dome tent, which is free but leaks a little when it rains.
Option two is renting a small cabin at the campground for about sixty dollars a night.
Then there's sleeping in the back of the van with a mattress, which my brother swears by.
Or finally, we buy a brand new tent, which is maybe two hundred dollars.
moshi_comment: The cabin is the safest bet if rain is likely, and over a weekend it costs less than a new tent. If you camp often, though, buying the new tent pays off quickly.
I'd try the van first, it's free and dry, as long as it's long enough to stretch out. The leaky dome tent is fine only if the forecast looks clear. How many nights are you going for?

option_sets.lead_in: I'm about to buy a tent and I keep going back and forth between three of them.
options: There's a big cabin-style tent for six, tall enough to stand up in, but it weighs almost thirty pounds.
Another is a light two-person backpacking tent, barely four pounds, though it's snug once the gear is inside.
Then there's a pop-up tent that sets itself up in seconds and it's cheap, but reviews say it struggles in wind.
moshi_comment: It really depends on how you camp. If you drive right to your pitch, the cabin tent's comfort is hard to beat, but the backpacking one is the only sensible pick if you'll carry it. I'd be wary of the pop-up if your sites get windy.
The pop-up is tempting for the price, but a tent that fails in wind can wreck a night. Between the other two, go big for family car trips, or light if you're hiking in.

option_sets.lead_in: We're picking a summer camping trip with the kids and there are a few ideas on the table.
options: A big holiday park with a pool, a kids club and a pizza van, about two hours from home.
A farm site where the kids can feed goats and collect eggs, very basic, just a field and a cold tap.
Island camping, which means a ferry ride, a beach almost to ourselves, and carrying everything from the dock.
Or the forest site we went to as kids, which my mum swears hasn't changed in thirty years.
moshi_comment: For younger kids the farm sounds magic, animals beat a pool most days, as long as you can live with the cold tap. The island is the big adventure, but hauling everything off a ferry with kids is real work.

The holiday park is the easy option and the kids will love the pool, but it might feel like any other holiday. If you want a story they'll tell for years, the island or your old forest site have more of that.

option_sets.lead_in: I need a camp stove and the guy at the shop gave me three choices.
options: A tiny canister stove that screws onto a gas can, super light, but it only fits one small pot.
A two-burner propane stove in a case, like a mini kitchen, heavy but you can cook a full breakfast on it.
A wood-burning stove that runs on twigs, so no fuel to buy, but it's fiddly and a bit smoky.
moshi_comment: If you mostly car camp with a group, the two-burner is the one you'll actually enjoy using. The canister stove is great for solo hikes, and the wood one is fun but frustrating when everything's damp.
I'd go canister if you ever carry your gear, it boils water fast and weighs nothing. The two-burner only makes sense next to the car, and the twig stove is more of a hobby than a reliable cooker.
